transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?

Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. Um... well, I guess I came in because I just keep feeling like... like I’ve completely let my family down by taking on this mortgage. It's just a lot of pressure, you know? And the house has this huge oak tree in the front yard. The real estate agent swore it was a selling point, but honestly it just drops these giant acorns everywhere. I was out there raking for three hours last week, and my neighbor brought out this gas-powered leaf blower. Loudest thing I've ever heard, and he didn't even look over to say hi. Just blew dust everywhere across the property line. 

But... yeah, anyway, the mortgage. I just feel like every small mistake I make at work—like if I forget a table's extra napkins or punch in an order wrong—it just proves I’m completely useless. Like I just deserve whatever happens to me at this point.
How long have you been feeling this way about yourself?

Um, let's see... I think the whole feeling like I'm just a burden and so guilty about everything, that's been going on for about a year and two months now? Give or take. It started around the time they changed the uniform policy at the restaurant. We used to wear these comfortable black polos, but then management decided we needed to look more "upscale," so they made us buy these stiff, white button-down shirts. White! At an Italian place! Do you know how hard it is to get marinara sauce out of a white collar? I was buying bleach by the gallon. And the fabric doesn't breathe at all, so when the kitchen gets backed up and you're running plates out to the patio, you're just sweating right through it. The patio gets full sun after 3 PM, too, because they cut down the awning to put up some string lights that don't even work half the time... 

But, yeah, I'd say about a year and a couple of months of feeling this way.
During these past fourteen months, have there been any periods of at least two months where you felt like your mood and energy were back to your normal, baseline self?

Um, two whole months? No... no, I don't think so. I mean, even when some days were a little lighter, like... well, like around Thanksgiving maybe. We actually had a decent tip out that week because management tried this new prix fixe menu for the holidays. Though, honestly, half the customers were absolutely furious they couldn't just order regular spaghetti and meatballs. 

This one guy in my section—section four, which is right by the swinging kitchen doors—he just kept snapping his fingers at me every time I walked past. And those doors, they swing out so wide they constantly hit the back of chair 42 if someone pushes them too hard from the back line. I kept trying to warn him to scoot his chair in, but he wouldn't listen, just kept snapping for more bread. People really don't treat you like a human being when you're carrying a tray, you know? They just see someone to boss around, and it's like they leave their manners in their cars... 

But, um, what were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling normal. Yeah, no, for most of this whole period, I’ve just been weighed down by that empty, guilty feeling more often than not. It never really went away for two months.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your appetite or your weight during this past year?

Um, yeah, my eating has been pretty all over the place, actually. Like, some weeks I barely even touch the staff meal. Which is a shame because Chef Tony makes this incredible chicken piccata on Tuesdays. Well, he used to. Now they’ve got him on this strict food cost budget, so it’s mostly just baked ziti. And the ziti is always dry because they leave it under the heat lamps way too long. The heat lamps in the expo window are ancient—one of the bulbs has been flickering since last October and nobody bothers to change it. It gives me a headache if I stare at it too long while waiting for my tickets. 

But, um, yeah, then other nights I'll come home after a closing shift, and I'll just eat whatever’s in the kitchen just to feel settled, you know? Like I'll stand in front of the fridge at 1 AM and just eat cold leftovers. My fridge has this weird hum, by the way. It sounds like a lawnmower running three blocks away. I asked the landlord to look at it, but he just said it's "character." Character doesn't keep the milk from freezing in the back left corner, but whatever. But yeah, my appetite is just... it's really up and down.

During this year-long period, have there been times where you felt so low that you experienced a significant loss of interest or pleasure in nearly all of your usual activities for at least two weeks at a time?

Um, yeah... yeah, definitely. I mean, most days there's just this heavy, empty feeling sitting right in my chest. Like I'm just going through the motions, you know? I'm out there carrying plates, refilling water glasses, and smiling at the tables, but I'm only doing it because I'm supposed to. I don't actually feel anything good. It's just exhausting. 

And speaking of exhausting, rolling silverware at the end of the night is the absolute worst when you feel like that. They make us use these cheap paper bands now instead of the cloth napkins, and the bands never stick right. You have to lick them, which is disgusting, or use this little sponge thing that always dries out halfway through the shift. And they expect us to roll like fifty sets before we can even clock out. I was sitting at the back booth—booth 12, the one with the tear in the vinyl that pinches your leg if you slide in too fast—just staring at this mountain of forks and knives, and I couldn't even bring myself to care. The forks aren't even all the same pattern anymore because the dishwasher keeps losing them in the drain trap... 

But, um, yeah. It’s been like that for weeks at a time. Just... empty. No interest in anything.
